claim: McrBC systems are among the most common forms of prokaryotic Type IV restriction systems.
source: A comprehensive census of McrBC systems, among the most common forms of prokaryotic Type IV restriction systems, followed by phylogenetic analysis, reveals their enormous abundance in diverse prokaryotes and a plethora of genomic associations.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of McrBC systems.

claim: CoCoNuTs show extraordinary variety, with three distinct types and multiple subtypes.
source: The CoCoNuTs alone show extraordinary variety, with three distinct types and multiple subtypes.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by the phylogenetic analysis and classification presented in the manuscript.

claim: All CoCoNuTs contain domains predicted to interact with translation system components.
source: All CoCoNuTs contain domains predicted to interact with translation system components, such as OB-folds resembling the SmpB protein that binds bacterial transfer-messenger RNA (tmRNA), YTH-like domains that might recognize methylated tmRNA, tRNA, or rRNA, and RNA-binding Hsp70 chaperone homologs, along with RNases, such as HEPN domains, all suggesting that the CoCoNuTs target RNA.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by domain analysis and structural predictions throughout the manuscript.

claim: CoCoNuTs are predicted to target RNA.
source: All CoCoNuTs contain domains predicted to interact with translation system components, such as OB-folds resembling the SmpB protein that binds bacterial transfer-messenger RNA (tmRNA), YTH-like domains that might recognize methylated tmRNA, tRNA, or rRNA, and RNA-binding Hsp70 chaperone homologs, along with RNases, such as HEPN domains, all suggesting that the CoCoNuTs target RNA.
evidence: This prediction is based on the presence of RNA-binding domains and RNases in CoCoNuT systems.

claim: Many CoCoNuTs might additionally target DNA via McrC nuclease homologs.
source: Many CoCoNuTs might additionally target DNA, via McrC nuclease homologs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract based on the presence of McrC nuclease domains in some CoCoNuT systems.

claim: Additional restriction systems such as Type I RM, BREX, and Druantia Type III are frequently encoded in the same predicted superoperons as CoCoNuTs.
source: Additional restriction systems, such as Type I RM, BREX, and Druantia Type III, are frequently encoded in the same predicted superoperons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by genomic neighborhood analysis throughout the manuscript.

claim: In many CoCoNuT superoperons, CoCoNuTs are likely regulated by cyclic nucleotides that bind associated CARF domains.
source: In many of these superoperons, CoCoNuTs are likely regulated by cyclic nucleotides, possibly, RNA fragments with cyclic termini, that bind associated CARF (CRISPR-Associated Rossmann Fold) domains.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract based on the presence of CARF domains in CoCoNuT genomic neighborhoods.

claim: The cyclic nucleotides that regulate CoCoNuTs are possibly RNA fragments with cyclic termini.
source: In many of these superoperons, CoCoNuTs are likely regulated by cyclic nucleotides, possibly, RNA fragments with cyclic termini, that bind associated CARF (CRISPR-Associated Rossmann Fold) domains.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the similarity of associated CARF domains to RtcR.

claim: CoCoNuTs employ an echeloned defense strategy analogous to that of Type III CRISPR-Cas systems.
source: We hypothesize that the CoCoNuTs, together with the ancillary restriction factors, employ an echeloned defense strategy analogous to that of Type III CRISPR-Cas systems, in which an immune response eliminating virus DNA and/or RNA is launched first, but then, if it fails, an abortive infection response leading to PCD/dormancy via host RNA cleavage takes over.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the abstract based on the genomic organization and domain composition of CoCoNuT systems.

claim: The continuous arms race between hosts and parasites drove the evolution of diverse defense systems in prokaryotes.
source: Over billions of years, the continuous arms race between hosts and parasites drove the evolution of immense, intricately interconnected networks of diverse defense systems and pathways (Burroughs et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2020; Goldfarb et al., 2015; Bell et al., 2020; Koonin and Aravind, 2002; Swarts et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Targeted searches for defense systems in prokaryotes have dramatically expanded their known diversity in recent years.
source: In particular, in the last few years, targeted searches for defense systems in prokaryotes, typically capitalizing on the presence of variable genomic defense islands, have dramatically expanded their known diversity and led to the discovery of a plethora of biological conflict strategies and mechanisms (Gao et al., 2020; Bell et al., 2020; Anantharaman et al., 2012; Kaur et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The McrBC system was the first form of restriction to be described.
source: Historically, the two-component McrBC (modified cytosine restriction) system was the first form of restriction to be described, although the mechanism remained obscure for decades, and for a time, this system was referred to as RglB (restriction of glucoseless phages) due to its ability to restrict T-even phage DNA which contained hydroxymethylcytosine, but not glucosylated bases (Raleigh et al., 1989; Luria and Human, 1952; Fleischman et al., 1976; Dila et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by historical citations.

claim: The prototypical McrBC system from E. coli K-12 is a Type IV restriction system that degrades DNA containing methylcytosine or hydroxymethylcytosine.
source: Today, the prototypical McrBC system, native to Escherichia coil K-12, is considered a Type IV (modification-dependent) restriction system that degrades DNA containing methylcytosine (5mC) or hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC), with a degree of sequence context specificity (Sutherland et al., 1992; Sukackaite et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Type IV restriction enzymes contain at least two components: a dedicated specificity domain that recognizes modified DNA and an endonuclease domain that cleaves the target.
source: Type IV restriction enzymes contain at least two components: (1) a dedicated specificity domain that recognizes modified DNA and (2) an endonuclease domain that cleaves the target (Weigele and Raleigh, 2016; Loenen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: In E. coli K-12 McrBC, McrB harbors an N-terminal DUF3578 (ADAM) domain that recognizes methylcytosine.
source: In the well-characterized example from E. coli K-12, McrB harbors an N-terminal DUF (domain of unknown function) 3578 that recognizes methylcytosine. We denote this domain, as its function is not unknown, as ADAM (a domain with an affinity for methylcytosine).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on known function of the domain.

claim: The ADAM domain in McrB is fused to a GTPase domain of the AAA+ATPase superfamily.
source: The ADAM domain is fused to a GTPase domain of the AAA+ATPase superfamily, the only known GTPase in this clade, which is believed to translocate DNA (Figure 1A and B; Sutherland et al., 1992; Iyer et al., 2004a; Nirwan et al., 2019; Panne et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1, supported by citations.

claim: The McrB GTPase is the only known GTPase in the AAA+ATPase clade.
source: The ADAM domain is fused to a GTPase domain of the AAA+ATPase superfamily, the only known GTPase in this clade, which is believed to translocate DNA (Figure 1A and B; Sutherland et al., 1992; Iyer et al., 2004a; Nirwan et al., 2019; Panne et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The McrB GTPase is believed to translocate DNA.
source: The ADAM domain is fused to a GTPase domain of the AAA+ATPase superfamily, the only known GTPase in this clade, which is believed to translocate DNA (Figure 1A and B; Sutherland et al., 1992; Iyer et al., 2004a; Nirwan et al., 2019; Panne et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: McrC contains an N-terminal DUF2357 domain that interacts with the GTPase domain in McrB and stimulates its activity.
source: McrC, encoded by a separate gene in the same operon, contains an N-terminal DUF2357 domain, which interacts with the GTPase domain in McrB and stimulates its activity, and is fused to a PD-(D/E)xK superfamily endonuclease (Figure 1A and C; Niu et al., 2020; Sutherland et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1, supported by citations.

claim: McrC is fused to a PD-(D/E)xK superfamily endonuclease.
source: McrC, encoded by a separate gene in the same operon, contains an N-terminal DUF2357 domain, which interacts with the GTPase domain in McrB and stimulates its activity, and is fused to a PD-(D/E)xK superfamily endonuclease (Figure 1A and C; Niu et al., 2020; Sutherland et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1, supported by citations.

claim: EVE superfamily domains in eukaryotes recognize modified DNA or RNA as part of mRNA maturation or epigenetic silencing functions.
source: EVE superfamily domains, which in eukaryotes recognize modified DNA or RNA as part of mRNA maturation or epigenetic silencing functions, are often fused to McrB-like GTPases in prokaryotes, and indeed, these are the most frequently occurring EVE-containing fusion proteins (Bell et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: EVE superfamily domains are often fused to McrB-like GTPases in prokaryotes.
source: EVE superfamily domains, which in eukaryotes recognize modified DNA or RNA as part of mRNA maturation or epigenetic silencing functions, are often fused to McrB-like GTPases in prokaryotes, and indeed, these are the most frequently occurring EVE-containing fusion proteins (Bell et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: McrB-like GTPases fused to EVE domains are the most frequently occurring EVE-containing fusion proteins.
source: EVE superfamily domains, which in eukaryotes recognize modified DNA or RNA as part of mRNA maturation or epigenetic silencing functions, are often fused to McrB-like GTPases in prokaryotes, and indeed, these are the most frequently occurring EVE-containing fusion proteins (Bell et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The comprehensive search identified nearly 34,000 McrBC systems distributed broadly among prokaryotes.
source: The search for McrBC systems included PSI-BLAST runs against the non-redundant protein sequence database at the NCBI, followed by several filtering strategies (see 'Methods') to obtain a clean set of nearly 34,000, distributed broadly among prokaryotes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the census methodology.

claim: Both the GTPase domains and DUF2357 domains frequently contained insertions into their coding sequences.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that both the GTPase domains and DUF2357 domains frequently contained insertions into their coding sequences, likely encoding specificity domains and coiled-coils, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequence analysis.

claim: The insertions in GTPase domains likely encode specificity domains.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that both the GTPase domains and DUF2357 domains frequently contained insertions into their coding sequences, likely encoding specificity domains and coiled-coils, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of domain insertions.

claim: The insertions in DUF2357 domains likely encode coiled-coils.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that both the GTPase domains and DUF2357 domains frequently contained insertions into their coding sequences, likely encoding specificity domains and coiled-coils, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of domain insertions.

claim: The phylogenetic trees of McrB GTPase and McrC DUF2357 families are generally topologically concordant.
source: Removing variable inserts from the conserved McrBC domains allowed accurate, comprehensive phylogenetic analysis of the McrB GTPase (Figure 2) and McrC DUF2357 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) families. These two trees were generally topologically concordant and revealed several distinct branches not previously recognized.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The phylogenetic analysis revealed several distinct branches of McrBC systems not previously recognized.
source: These two trees were generally topologically concordant and revealed several distinct branches not previously recognized.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The branch containing the prototypical E. coli K-12 McrBC system is characterized by frequent genomic association with Type I RM systems.
source: The branch containing the prototypical McrBC system from E. coil K-12 (Figure 2, blue) is characterized by frequent genomic association with Type I RM systems, usually with unidirectional gene orientations and the potential of forming a single operon (Raleigh, 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2, supported by a citation.

claim: A major branch of the McrBC family is characterized by a conserved deletion within the NxxD GTPase signature motif, reducing it to NxD.
source: A major branch (Figure 2, teal and yellow) of the McrBC family is characterized by a conserved deletion within the NxxD GTPase signature motif (where x is any amino acid), found in all McrB-like GTPases, reducing it to NxD (Figures 1B and 2; Neuwald et al., 1999; Iyer et al., 2004a; Erzberger and Berger, 2006; Niu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2, supported by citations.

claim: The NxD variant of the motif is strictly conserved in NxD branch homologs.
source: The NxD variant of the motif is strictly conserved in these homologs and is usually, but not invariably, followed by a glutamate (E) or a second aspartate (D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequence analysis.

claim: The asparagine residue in the NxxD motif is strictly required for GTP binding and hydrolysis.
source: The asparagine (N) residue is strictly required for GTP binding and hydrolysis (Pieper et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The asparagine residue in the NxxD motif is analogous to sensor-1 in ATP-hydrolyzing members of the AAA+ family.
source: As this residue is analogous to sensor-1 in ATP-hydrolyzing members of the AAA+family, it can be predicted to position a catalytic water molecule for nucleophilic attack on the γ-phosphate of an NTP (Erzberger and Berger, 2006; Colicelli, 2004; Bourne et al., 1991; Niu et al., 2020; Pieper et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The aspartate in the NxxD motif interacts with a conserved arginine/lysine residue in McrC.
source: A recent structural analysis has shown that the aspartate interacts with a conserved arginine/lysine residue in McrC which, via a hydrogen-bonding network, resituates the NxxD motif in relation to its interface with the Walker B motif such that, together, they optimally position a catalytic water to stimulate hydrolysis (Niu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The truncation of the NxxD motif to NxD might modulate the rate of GTP hydrolysis.
source: Accordingly, the truncation of this motif might be expected to modulate the rate of hydrolysis and potentially compel functional association with only a subset of McrC homologs containing compensatory mutations.
evidence: This is a prediction based on structural and functional analysis of the motif.

claim: The most notable feature of the NxD branch of GTPases is a large clade characterized by fusion to long coiled-coil domains.
source: The most notable feature of the NxD branch of GTPases is a large clade characterized by fusion to long coiled-coil domains (Figure 2, teal; Supplementary file 1), a derived and distinctly different architecture from the small, modular DNA-binding specificity domains typically found in canonical McrB homologs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The McrC homologs associated with coiled-coil McrB-like GTPase fusions often lack the PD-(D/E)xK endonuclease entirely or contain an inactivated version.
source: The McrC homologs associated with these coiled-coil McrB-like GTPase fusions also often lack the PD-(D/E)xK endonuclease entirely or contain a region AlphaFold2 (AF2) predicted to adopt the PD-(D/E)xK endonuclease fold, but with inactivating replacements of catalytic residues (Supplementary file 1; Jumper et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural predictions and sequence analysis.

claim: When the McrC nuclease is missing or likely inactive in CoCoNuT systems, these systems are always encoded in close association with HEPN ribonuclease domains or other predicted nucleases.
source: However, in the cases where the McrC nuclease is missing or likely inactive, these systems are always encoded in close association, often with overlapping reading frames, with HEPN (higher eukaryotes and prokaryotes nucleotide-binding) ribonuclease domains, or other predicted nucleases (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Pillon et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3, supported by a citation.

claim: CoCoNuT systems are extremely diverse and represented in a wide variety of bacteria, particularly Pseudomonadota and Bacillota.
source: CoCoNuT systems are extremely diverse and represented in a wide variety of bacteria, particularly Pseudomonadota and Bacillota, but are nearly absent in archaea (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: CoCoNuT systems are nearly absent in archaea.
source: CoCoNuT systems are extremely diverse and represented in a wide variety of bacteria, particularly Pseudomonadota and Bacillota, but are nearly absent in archaea (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: CoCoNuTs were classified into three types and seven subtypes based on GTPase domain phylogeny and conserved genomic context.
source: We classified the CoCoNuTs into three types and seven subtypes based on the GTPase domain phylogeny and conserved genomic context (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Type I-A CoCoNuT is distinguished from all other CoCoNuTs by a helical insert into the CnuB GTPase domain between the Walker B and NxD motifs.
source: Type I-A is distinguished from all other CoCoNuTs by a helical insert into the CnuB GTPase domain, between the Walker B and NxD motifs (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Type I-B systems usually encode a separate coiled-coil protein CnuA in addition to CnuB/McrB and CnuC/McrC.
source: Type I-B systems usually encode a separate coiled-coil protein, which we denote CnuA, in addition to CnuB/McrB and CnuC/McrC, with no coiled-coil fused to the GTPase domain in CnuB (Figures 3 and 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: CnuA in Type I-B CoCoNuTs is fused at the N-terminus to a pyrin/CARD-like helical domain and at the C-terminus to a phosphoacceptor receiver domain.
source: CnuA is fused at the N-terminus to a pyrin (PYD)/CARD (caspase activation and recruitment domain)-like helical domain and at the C-terminus to a phosphoacceptor receiver (REC) domain (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The association of PYD/CARD-like domains with CoCoNuTs suggests involvement in a programmed cell death/abortive infection-type response.
source: The association of the PYD/CARD-like domains with CoCoNuTs suggests involvement in a programmed cell death (PCD)/abortive infection-type response as they belong to the DEATH domain superfamily and are best characterized in the context of innate immunity, inflammasome formation, and PCD (Park et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of PYD/CARD domains, supported by a citation.

claim: REC domains constitute one of the components of two-component regulatory systems and are targeted for phosphorylation by histidine kinases.
source: The REC domains constitute one of the components of two-component regulatory systems. They are targeted for phosphorylation by histidine kinases (Stock et al., 2000), which could be a mechanism of Type I-B CoCoNuT regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Cold shock domain-like OB-folds are usually fused at the N-termini of Type I CoCoNuT CnuB/McrB proteins.
source: In contrast to Type II and Type III CnuB GTPase homologs, which contain only coiled-coils fused at their N-termini (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1), cold shock domain (CSD)-like OB-folds are usually fused at the N-termini of Type I CoCoNuT CnuB/McrB proteins, in addition to the coiled-coils (except for Type I-B, where the coiled-coils are encoded separately) (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1; Amir et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: A YTH-like domain is often present in Type I-B and I-C CnuB, between the CSD and coiled-coil or between the CSD and the GTPase domain.
source: Often, in Type I-B and I-C, but not Type I-A, a YTH-like domain, a member of the modified base-binding EVE superfamily, is present in CnuB as well, between the CSD and coiled-coil, or in Type I-B, between the CSD and the GTPase domain (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1; Bell et al., 2020; Hazra et al., 2019; Liao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5, supported by citations.

claim: All Type I CoCoNuT CnuC/McrC proteins contain an immunoglobulin-like N-terminal beta-sandwich domain.
source: The CnuC/McrC proteins in Type I CoCoNuTs, as well as those in Type II and Types III-B and III-C, all contain an immunoglobulin-like N-terminal beta-sandwich domain of unknown function, not present in the E. coli K-12 McrC homolog, similar to a wide range of folds from this superfamily with diverse roles (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplements 1–4, Supplementary file 1; Anonymous, 2015; Halaby et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The immunoglobulin-like beta-sandwich domain is also present in non-CoCoNuT McrC homologs associated with McrB GTPase homologs in the NxD clade.
source: It is also present in non-CoCoNuT McrC homologs associated with McrB GTPase homologs in the NxD clade, implying its function is not specific to the CoCoNuTs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequence analysis.

claim: In Type I-B and I-C CoCoNuT CnuC homologs, the immunoglobulin-like domains most closely resemble Rho GDP-dissociation inhibitor 1.
source: In the Type I-B and I-C CoCoNuT CnuC homologs, these domains most closely resemble Rho GDP-dissociation inhibitor 1, suggesting that they may be involved in the regulation of CnuB/McrB GTPase activity (Dovas and Couchman, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural similarity, supported by a citation.

claim: Pseudo-Type I-B CoCoNuTs are hypothesized to play a role in overcrowding-induced stress responses.
source: We hypothesize that Pseudo-Type I-B CoCoNuTs play a role in overcrowding-induced stress responses. We inferred this functional prediction from the fact that the islands in which they occur typically also encode a quorum-sensing hormone synthase, a mechanosensitive ion channel, various transporters, antibiotic resistance and synthesis factors, and cell wall-related proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on genomic context analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Type II and III CoCoNuT CnuB/McrB GTPase domains are encoded in a nearly completely conserved genomic association with a Superfamily 1 helicase of the UPF1-like clade (CnuH).
source: Type II and III CoCoNuT CnuB/McrB GTPase domains branch from within Type I-A and are encoded in a nearly completely conserved genomic association with a Superfamily 1 (SF1) helicase of the UPF1-like clade, which we denote CnuH (Figure 3, Supplementary file 1; Gorbalenya and Koonin, 1993; Fairman-Williams et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3, supported by citations.

claim: The UPF1-like family encompasses helicases with diverse functions acting on RNA and single-stranded DNA substrates.
source: The UPF1-like family encompasses helicases with diverse functions acting on RNA and single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) substrates, and notably, the prototypical UPF1 RNA helicase and its closest relatives are highly conserved in eukaryotes, where they play a critical role in the nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) RNA surveillance pathway (Cheng et al., 2007; Chakrabarti et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The prototypical UPF1 RNA helicase plays a critical role in the nonsense-mediated decay RNA surveillance pathway in eukaryotes.
source: The UPF1-like family encompasses helicases with diverse functions acting on RNA and single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) substrates, and notably, the prototypical UPF1 RNA helicase and its closest relatives are highly conserved in eukaryotes, where they play a critical role in the nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) RNA surveillance pathway (Cheng et al., 2007; Chakrabarti et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: In all four Type II and Type III CoCoNuT subtypes, the CnuH helicases contain a large helical insertion following the Walker A motif.
source: In all four Type II and Type III CoCoNuT subtypes, following the Walker A motif, the CnuH helicases contain a large helical insertion, with some of the helices predicted to form coiled-coils (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Type II, Type III-A, and Type III-B CoCoNuT CnuH helicases contain an OB-fold domain.
source: The Type II, Type III-A, and Type III-B CoCoNuT CnuH helicases contain an OB-fold domain that, in Type II and Type III-A, is flanked by helices predicted to form a stalk-like helical extension of the N-terminal RecA-like domain, a structural feature characteristic of the entire UPF1/DNA2-like helicase family within SF1 (Chakrabarti et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2015; Kalathiya et al., 2019; Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6, supported by citations.

claim: The CnuH-predicted OB-fold domain in Type II CoCoNuTs is similar to the OB-fold domain in UPF1 and related RNA helicases SMUBP-2 and SEN1.
source: DALI comparisons show that the CnuH-predicted OB-fold domain in Type II CoCoNuTs is similar to the OB-fold domain in UPF1 and related RNA helicases SMUBP-2 and SEN1, and this holds for Type III-A as well, although, in these systems, the best DALI hits are to translation factor components such as EF-Tu domain II (Supplementary file 1; Chakrabarti et al., 2011; Morse et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural comparison.

claim: In Type II and Type III-A CoCoNuTs, CnuH is fused at the N-terminus to a second OB-fold domain similar to that of SmpB.
source: In Type II and Type III-A CoCoNuTs, CnuH is fused at the N-terminus to a second OB-fold domain similar to that of SmpB (small protein B) (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and, 5, Supplementary file 1), which we denote SPB (SmpB-like).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: SmpB binds to SsrA RNA (tmRNA) and is required for tmRNA to rescue stalled ribosomes.
source: SmpB binds to SsrA RNA, also known as transfer-messenger RNA (tmRNA), and is required for tmRNA to rescue stalled ribosomes, via entry into their A-sites with its alanine-charged tRNA-like domain (Barends et al., 2001; Himeno et al., 2014; Guyomar et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The SPB domain is around 20 amino acids shorter on average than SmpB itself.
source: The SPB domain is around 20 amino acids shorter on average than SmpB itself, and a helix that is conserved in SmpB orthologs and interacts with the tmRNA is absent in the CoCoNuT OB folds (Figure 6—figure supplement 5; Bessho et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: Two structural elements of SmpB involved in binding tmRNA are present in the SPB domain.
source: However, two other structural elements of SmpB involved in binding tmRNA are present (Figure 6—figure supplement 5; Gutmann et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5, supported by a citation.

claim: The Type II and Type III-A CoCoNuT CnuH helicases contain an RNase toxin-like domain located between the SPB OB-fold and the helicase.
source: The Type II and Type III-A CoCoNuT CnuH helicases contain an additional domain, structurally similar to the RelE/Colicin D RNase fold (Gucinski et al., 2019), which we denote RNase toxin-like (RTL), located between the SPB OB-fold and the helicase (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6, supported by a citation.

claim: The RTL domain was identified by structural similarity search with AF2 models, but no sequence conservation with characterized members of this family was detected.
source: This domain was identified by structural similarity search with the AF2 models, but no sequence conservation with characterized members of this family was detected, leaving it uncertain whether the RTL domain is an active nuclease.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: In Type III-B CoCoNuTs, a wHTH domain resembling the archaeal ssDNA-binding protein Sul7s is fused to the CnuH N-termini.
source: In Type III-B CoCoNuTs, a wHTH domain resembling the archaeal ssDNA-binding protein Sul7s is fused to the CnuH N-termini (Figure 6, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Helicases of the UPF1-like family are typically encoded in operons with downstream genes coding for an elongated wHTH domain fused to various effectors, generally nucleases (CnuE).
source: Our observations of the contextual associations, both of the CoCoNuTs and their relatives, showed that helicases of this large family are typically encoded in operons with downstream genes coding for an elongated wHTH domain fused at its C-terminus to a variety of effectors, generally, nucleases, which we denote CnuE (Figures 3 and 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 3 and 6.

claim: In Type II and Type III-A CoCoNuTs, the CnuE effectors are HEPN ribonucleases.
source: In the CoCoNuTs, except for Types III-B and III-C, these CnuE effectors are HEPN ribonucleases, with one HEPN domain in Type II and two in Type III-A (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: In Type III-B CoCoNuTs, the effector is a Vsr-like PD-(D/E)xK family endonuclease fused directly to the helicase.
source: In Type III-B, the effector is a Vsr (very-short-patch repair)-like PD-(D/E)xK family endonuclease (Tsutakawa et al., 1999) fused directly to the helicase, with no wHTH domain present, whereas in Type III-C, a distorted version of the elongated wHTH domain is fused to two phospholipase D (PLD) family endonuclease domains (Figure 6, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6, supported by a citation.

claim: In Type III-C CoCoNuTs, a distorted version of the elongated wHTH domain is fused to two phospholipase D family endonuclease domains.
source: In Type III-B, the effector is a Vsr (very-short-patch repair)-like PD-(D/E)xK family endonuclease (Tsutakawa et al., 1999) fused directly to the helicase, with no wHTH domain present, whereas in Type III-C, a distorted version of the elongated wHTH domain is fused to two phospholipase D (PLD) family endonuclease domains (Figure 6, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: All the nucleases associated with CoCoNuT CnuE proteins can degrade RNA.
source: All these nucleases can degrade RNA, and some, such as HEPN, have been found to cleave RNA exclusively (Pillon et al., 2021; Ipsaro et al., 2012; Mendez et al., 2018; Laganeckas et al., 2011; Songailiene et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: HEPN nucleases have been found to cleave RNA exclusively.
source: All these nucleases can degrade RNA, and some, such as HEPN, have been found to cleave RNA exclusively (Pillon et al., 2021; Ipsaro et al., 2012; Mendez et al., 2018; Laganeckas et al., 2011; Songailiene et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Multimer structural modeling with AF2 suggests that the wHTH domain in CnuE might interact with the coiled-coil-containing helical insertion of CnuH.
source: Multimer structural modeling with AF2 suggests that the wHTH domain in CnuE might interact with the coiled-coil-containing helical insertion of CnuH, perhaps mediated by the coiled-coils in each protein, to couple the ATP-driven helicase activity to the various nuclease effectors (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural modeling shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Type II and Type III-A CoCoNuTs include conserved genes coding for a 'TerY-P' triad.
source: Type II and Type III-A CoCoNuTs, the most widespread varieties apart from Type I, also include conserved genes coding for a 'TerY-P' triad. TerY-P consists of a TerY-like von Willebrand factor type A (VWA) domain, a protein phosphatase 2C-like enzyme, and a serine/threonine kinase (STK) fused at the C-terminus to a zinc ribbon (ZnR) (Figure 3, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: TerY-P triads are involved in tellurite resistance and are hypothesized to function as a metal-sensing phosphorylation-dependent signaling switch.
source: TerY-P triads are involved in tellurite resistance, associated with various predicted DNA restriction and processing systems, and are hypothesized to function as a metal-sensing phosphorylation-dependent signaling switch (Anantharaman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Almost all CoCoNuT systems containing cnuHE operons also encompass TerY-P.
source: Almost all CoCoNuT systems containing cnuHE operons also encompass TerY-P, with a few exceptions among Terrabacterial Type II systems and Myxococcal Type III-A systems, implying an important contribution to their function (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on genomic analysis.

claim: The complete absence of the TerY-P module in Type III-B and Type III-C systems suggests that when different nucleases and other putative effectors fused to the helicase are present, TerY-P is dispensable for the CoCoNuT activity.
source: However, the complete absence of the TerY-P module in Type III-B and Type III-C systems suggests that when different nucleases and other putative effectors fused to the helicase are present, TerY-P is dispensable for the CoCoNuT activity. Therefore, we do not consider them to be core components of these systems.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of TerY-P in certain CoCoNuT types.

claim: Type II CnuC/McrC homologs resemble Type I-A CnuCs but have undergone reductive evolution.
source: Type II CnuCs resemble Type I-A CnuCs, which contain N-terminal immunoglobulin-like beta-sandwich domains, PD-(D/E)xK nucleases, zinc ribbon domains, and insertions into DUF2357 containing coiled-coils and a CSD-like OBD. However, in Type II CnuCs, this domain architecture underwent reductive evolution (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2, Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: In Type II CnuCs, the beta-sandwich domain and coiled-coils are shorter, the CSD was lost, the nuclease domain was inactivated, and the number of Zn-binding CPxC motifs was often reduced from three to two.
source: In particular, the beta-sandwich domain and coiled-coils are shorter, the CSD was lost, the nuclease domain was inactivated, and, in many cases, the number of Zn-binding CPxC motifs was reduced from three to two (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2, Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Type III-A CnuC/McrC homologs entirely lost the beta-sandwich domain, PD-(D/E)xK nuclease, and zinc ribbon found in Type I-A and Type II.
source: By contrast, Type III-A CnuC/McrC homologs entirely lost the beta-sandwich domain, PD-(D/E)xK nuclease, and zinc ribbon found in Type I-A and Type II, but gained an Hsp70-like NBD/SBD unit similar to those fused to the McrB-like GTPase domain in early branching members of the NxD clade.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on domain analysis.

claim: Type III-A CnuC/McrC homologs gained an Hsp70-like NBD/SBD unit and a helical domain similar to the HEAT repeat family.
source: By contrast, Type III-A CnuC/McrC homologs entirely lost the beta-sandwich domain, PD-(D/E)xK nuclease, and zinc ribbon found in Type I-A and Type II, but gained an Hsp70-like NBD/SBD unit similar to those fused to the McrB-like GTPase domain in early branching members of the NxD clade. They have also acquired a helical domain similar to the HEAT repeat family, and, in some cases, a second CSD (Figures 3 and 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 4, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 3, 5, and 6.

claim: In Types III-B and III-C, the Hsp70-like ATPase NBD/SBD domains and HEAT-like repeats are encoded by a separate gene (CnuD).
source: Hsp70-like ATPase NBD/SBD domains and HEAT-like repeats are fused to the CnuC/McrC N-terminal DUF2357 domain in Type III-A CoCoNuT, but their homologs in Types III-B and III-C are encoded by a separate gene. We denote these proteins CnuD and CnuCD, the latter for the CnuC-CnuD fusions in Type III-A.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on genomic organization.

claim: The separation of CnuD domains in Types III-B and III-C implies that fusion is not required for their functional interaction with the CnuBC/McrBC systems.
source: The separation of these domains in Types III-B and III-C implies that fusion is not required for their functional interaction with the CnuBC/McrBC systems (Figures 3 and 6A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic organization shown in Figures 3 and 6.

claim: Walker B-like motifs are usually conserved in CnuD homologs, whereas Walker A-like motifs are present but degenerate.
source: In the CnuD homologs found in the CoCoNuTs and fused to NxD McrB GTPases, Walker B-like motifs (Yamamoto et al., 2014) are usually, but not invariably, conserved, whereas the sequences of the helical domains adjacent to the motifs are more strongly constrained. Walker A-like motifs (Chang et al., 2008) are present but degenerate (Figure 6—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 6, supported by citations.

claim: The CoCoNuT CnuD homologs likely bind ATP/ADP but hydrolyze ATP with extremely low efficiency, at best.
source: Therefore, it appears likely that the CoCoNuT CnuD homologs bind ATP/ADP but hydrolyze ATP with extremely low efficiency, at best.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of Walker motifs.

claim: The properties of CoCoNuT CnuD homologs are better compatible with RNA binding than unfolded protein binding or remodeling.
source: Such properties in an Hsp70-like domain are better compatible with RNA binding than unfolded protein binding or remodeling, suggesting that these CnuD homologs may target the respective systems to viral/aberrant RNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the Hsp70-like domain.

claim: Many Hsp70 homologs have been reported to associate with ribosomes.
source: Many Hsp70 homologs have been reported to associate with ribosomes (Mayer, 2021; Willmund et al., 2013), which could also be true for the CoCoNuT Cnu(C)Ds.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Type II and III-A CoCoNuTs likely target RNA rather than DNA.
source: Consistent with this prediction, Type II and III-A CoCoNuTs likely target RNA rather than DNA, given that the respective operons encode HEPN RNases, typically the only recognizable nuclease in these systems.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of HEPN RNases and absence of active DNA nucleases.

claim: All CnuC/McrC homologs in Type II or III CoCoNuT systems lack the PD-(D/E)xK catalytic motif required for nuclease activity.
source: All CnuC/McrC homologs in Type II or III CoCoNuT systems lack the PD-(D/E)xK catalytic motif that is required for nuclease activity, although for Type II and Types III-B and III-C, but not Type III-A, structural modeling indicates that the inactivated nuclease domain was retained, likely for a nucleic acid-binding role (Figure 6, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: In Type III-A CoCoNuT, the nuclease domain was lost entirely and replaced by the Hsp70-like NBD/SBD domain.
source: In Type III-A CoCoNuT, the nuclease domain was lost entirely and replaced by the Hsp70-like NBD/SBD domain with RNA-binding potential described above (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 4, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: RNA targeting is likely an ancestral feature of the CoCoNuT systems.
source: We suspect that RNA targeting is an ancestral feature of the CoCoNuT systems.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the Results section.

claim: In some Type III-A CoCoNuT subtypes, a CARF domain-containing protein is encoded, with two distinct CARF domains encompassing different RING nuclease motifs fused to a D-ExK nuclease domain.
source: In the first two of these Type III-A subtypes shown in Figure 7, a CARF (CRISPR-Associated Rossmann Fold) domain-containing protein is encoded, with two distinct CARF domains encompassing different RING nuclease motifs. These CARF domains are fused at the C-terminus to a D-ExK nuclease domain, an architecture suggestive of a PCD/dormancy-eliciting antiphage effector (Supplementary file 1; Makarova et al., 2014; Makarova et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7, supported by citations.

claim: Homologs of the CARF-D-ExK protein, Can1 and Can2, have been characterized as CRISPR ancillary nucleases.
source: Indeed, homologs of this protein, Can1 and Can2, have been characterized as CRISPR ancillary nucleases (McMahon et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2021), and Can2 has been reported to cleave both DNA and RNA (Zhu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Can2 has been reported to cleave both DNA and RNA.
source: Indeed, homologs of this protein, Can1 and Can2, have been characterized as CRISPR ancillary nucleases (McMahon et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2021), and Can2 has been reported to cleave both DNA and RNA (Zhu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: One variant of extended Type III-A CoCoNuTs includes an FtsK-like ATPase homologous to the Type VII secretion system factor EssC.
source: The first of the three variable regions flanked by the VWA domain-encoding genes includes an FtsK-like ATPase homologous to the Type VII secretion system factor EssC (Figure 7, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7.

claim: EssC contains three tandem ATPase domains with Walker A/B motifs required for ATP hydrolysis present only in D1 and D2.
source: EssC contains three tandem ATPase domains (D1, D2, and D3), with the Walker A/B motifs required for ATP hydrolysis present only in D1 and D2 (Warne et al., 2016; Bobrovskyy et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The CoCoNuT-associated EssC homologs possess three ATPase domains but only the central D2 domain homolog is predicted to be active.
source: The CoCoNuT-associated homologs also possess three ATPase domains but differ in that only the central D2 domain homolog is predicted to be active.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequence analysis.

claim: The region containing the EssC-like ATPase also codes for two WXG100 proteins and a coiled-coil fused to a restriction endonuclease-like domain with a D-ExK catalytic motif.
source: In addition, the region codes for two WXG100 proteins, one with the characteristic WxG motif and the other without (but with a similar predicted structure), as well as a coiled-coil fused to a restriction endonuclease-like domain with a D-ExK catalytic motif (Figure 7, Supplementary file 1; Poulsen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7, supported by a citation.

claim: WXG100 proteins are known to be secreted, with ESAT-6 being a T-cell antigen diagnostic of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.
source: It appears likely that some or all of these factors are secreted, especially the WXG100 proteins, which are known to be secreted, with the prototypical example, ESAT-6, being a T-cell antigen diagnostic of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection (Poulsen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The second variant of extended Type III-A CoCoNuTs encodes a SpoVK family of AAA+ATPases homologous to p97/CDC48.
source: In the second of these Type III-A CoCoNuT extensions with two VWA domains, a SpoVK family of AAA+ATPases homologous to p97/CDC48 is encoded adjacent to a protein containing a C-terminal bacteriocin-like glycine zipper motif (Figure 7, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7.

claim: CDC48 is involved in eukaryotic protein quality control, particularly the degradation of proteins synthesized from non-stop mRNA.
source: CDC48 is involved in eukaryotic protein quality control, particularly the degradation of proteins synthesized from non-stop mRNA, where it is required to release nascent polypeptides from stalled ribosomes to enable proteolysis (Verma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The CoCoNuT-associated CDC48 homologs contain tandem ATPases, but the Walker A/B motifs are conserved only in the C-terminal domain.
source: CDC48 contains two tandem ATPase domains, both of which are active; the CoCoNuT-associated homologs also contain tandem ATPases, but the Walker A/B motifs required to bind and hydrolyze ATP are conserved only in the C-terminal domain (Baek et al., 2013; Wolf and Stolz, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The third variant of extended Type III-A CoCoNuTs encodes a distinct member of the FtsK/HerA superfamily homologous to the ESX-3 Type VII secretion system factor EccE3.
source: The third variant of these extended Type III-A CoCoNuTs encodes a distinct member of the FtsK/HerA superfamily, which is also likely assembled into hexamers (Figure 7, Supplementary file 1; Iyer et al., 2004b). AF2 structural modeling suggests these enzymes are homologs of the ESX-3 Type VII secretion system factor EccE3 (Poweleit et al., 2019), albeit containing a unique beta-strand insertion of variable length.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7, supported by citations.

claim: The EccE3-like domain is fused to an ATPase domain similar to the Type IV secretion system protein VirB4.
source: This EccE3-like domain is fused to an ATPase domain similar to the Type IV secretion system protein VirB4, which is involved in bacterial conjugation (Figure 7, Supplementary file 1; Wallden et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7, supported by a citation.

claim: Type III-A CoCoNuTs in Helicobacter appear to be translated using an alternate genetic code.
source: While investigating this additional diversity of Type III-A CoCoNuTs, we observed that Type III-A CoCoNuTs in Helicobacter appeared to be translated using an alternate genetic code because gene predictions with the standard code divided the expected open-reading frames into many small fragments.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on gene prediction analysis.

claim: A novel type of conditional or otherwise complex translation regulation likely occurs in Helicobacter CoCoNuTs, perhaps triggered by phage infection.
source: We were unable to identify a known alternative code that would yield the expected CoCoNuT gene products. Thus, a novel type of conditional or otherwise complex translation regulation likely occurs in these species, perhaps triggered by phage infection (for the accessions of identifiable Type III-A CoCoNuT factors in Helicobacter, see Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the inability to identify a known alternative genetic code.

claim: Genomic neighborhoods of many Type II and Type III-A CoCoNuTs encompass complex operonic associations with genes encoding CARF domain-containing proteins.
source: Genomic neighborhoods of many Type II and Type III-A CoCoNuTs encompass complex operonic associations with genes encoding several types of CARF domain-containing proteins (Figures 7 and 8, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The connection with CARF domains suggests multifarious regulation by cyclic (oligo)nucleotide second messengers synthesized in response to viral infection.
source: This connection suggests multifarious regulation by cyclic (oligo)nucleotide second messengers synthesized in response to viral infection and bound by CARF domains (Makarova et al., 2020a; McMahon et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of CARF domains, supported by citations.

claim: Activation of an effector by a CARF bound to a cyclic (oligo)nucleotide is a crucial mechanism of CBASS and Type III CRISPR-Cas systems.
source: Activation of an effector, most often a nuclease, such as HEPN or PD-(D/E)xK, by a CARF bound to a cyclic (oligo)nucleotide is a crucial mechanism of CBASS (cyclic oligonucleotide-based antiphage signaling system) as well as Type III CRISPR-Cas systems (McMahon et al., 2020; Makarova et al., 2020a; Zhu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Most CoCoNuT-associated CARF domain-containing proteins showed the highest similarity to RtcR, a sigma54 transcriptional coactivator of the RNA repair system RtcAB.
source: Surprisingly, however, most of these CARF domain-containing proteins showed the highest similarity to RtcR, a sigma54 transcriptional coactivator of the RNA repair system RtcAB with a CARF-ATPase-HTH domain architecture, suggesting an alternative functional prediction (Figure 8, Figure 8—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8.

claim: By analogy with RtcR, CoCoNuT-associated CARF domain-containing proteins might bind (t)RNA fragments with 2′,3′ cyclic phosphate ends.
source: Specifically, by analogy with RtcR, CoCoNuT-associated CARF domain-containing proteins might bind (t)RNA fragments with 2′,3′ cyclic phosphate ends (Kotta-Loizou et al., 2022; Hughes et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a prediction based on similarity to RtcR, supported by citations.

claim: Binding of RNA fragments with cyclic phosphate ends could promote transcription of downstream CoCoNuT genes through binding an upstream activating sequence by the HTH domain.
source: This interaction could promote transcription of downstream genes, in this case, genes encoding CoCoNuT components, through binding an upstream activating sequence by the HTH domain fused to the CARF-ATPase C-terminus (Hughes et al., 2020; Kotta-Loizou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the mechanism of RtcR, supported by citations.

claim: Bacterial anticodon nucleases generate tRNA fragments in response to infection and DNA degradation by phages.
source: Lately, it has been shown that bacterial anticodon nucleases, in response to infection and DNA degradation by phages, generate tRNA fragments, likely a signal of infection and a defensive strategy to slow down the translation of viral mRNA, and that phages can deploy tRNA repair enzymes and other strategies to counteract this defense mechanism (Bitton et al., 2015; van den Berg et al., 2023; Kaufmann, 2000; Ishita et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The activity of HEPN ribonucleases in CoCoNuTs would produce RNA cleavage products with cyclic phosphate ends that might be bound by the associated RtcR-like CARFs.
source: Moreover, the activity of the HEPN ribonucleases in the CoCoNuTs themselves would produce RNA cleavage products with cyclic phosphate ends that might be bound by the associated RtcR-like CARFs (Shigematsu et al., 2018; Pillon et al., 2021), in a potential feedback loop.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the activity of HEPN nucleases, supported by citations.

claim: RtcA is an RNA cyclase that converts 3′-phosphate RNA termini to 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate.
source: Such a CoCoNuT mechanism could complement the function of RtcAB as RtcA is an RNA cyclase that converts 3′-phosphate RNA termini to 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate and thus, in a feedback loop, generates 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate RNA fragments that induce expression of the operon (Genschik et al., 1998; Das and Shuman, 2013; Hughes et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: RtcB is an RNA ligase that joins 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate RNA termini to 5′-OH RNA fragments.
source: Acting downstream of RtcA, RtcB is an RNA ligase that joins 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate RNA termini to 5′-OH RNA fragments, generating a 5′–3′ bond and, in many cases, reconstituting a functional tRNA (Tanaka and Shuman, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: In bacteria, the most frequent target of RtcB is SsrA, the tmRNA.
source: Recent work has shown that, in bacteria, the most frequent target of RtcB is SsrA, the tmRNA (Kotta-Loizou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: There are notable parallels between CoCoNuTs and Type III CRISPR-Cas systems.
source: There are notable parallels between CoCoNuTs and Type III CRISPR-Cas systems, where the Cas10-Csm-crRNA effector complex binds phage RNA complementary to the spacer of the crRNA, triggering both restriction of phage DNA and indiscriminate cleavage of RNA (McMahon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: In Type III CRISPR-Cas systems, target RNA recognition stimulates the production of cyclic oligoadenylate signal molecules by Cas10.
source: The target RNA recognition stimulates the production of cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA) signal molecules by Cas10, and these bind the CARF domain of PCD effectors, such as Csm6, activating their nuclease moieties, typically HEPN domains that function as promiscuous RNases (Pillon et al., 2021; Millman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: In Type III CRISPR-Cas systems, infection is either eradicated quickly by restriction of virus DNA or PCD/dormancy occurs via continued cOA signaling.
source: One of the two outcomes can result from this cascade: infection is either eradicated quickly by restriction of the virus DNA, which inhibits cOA signaling via the depletion of viral RNA, along with the activity of RING nucleases, thus averting PCD, or else, the continued presence of viral RNA stimulates cOA signaling until PCD or dormancy occurs, limiting the spread of viruses to neighboring cells in the bacterial population (Makarova et al., 2012; Koonin and Aravind, 2002; Koonin and Krupovic, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: In CARF-containing CoCoNuTs, binding of a 2′,3′ cyclic phosphate RNA fragment by the CARF domain would initiate the expression of the entire gene cluster.
source: In contrast, in the CARF-containing CoCoNuTs, both the DNA and RNA restriction factors appear to be arranged such that binding of a 2′,3′ cyclic phosphate RNA fragment by the CARF domain would initiate the expression of the entire gene cluster (McMahon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the genomic organization and similarity to RtcR, supported by a citation.

claim: In complex CoCoNuT configurations, the gene order is likely to be important, with Type I RM almost always directly following CARF genes and CoCoNuTs typically coming last.
source: In these complex configurations of the CoCoNuT genome neighborhoods (Figure 8), the gene order is likely to be important, with Type I RM almost always directly following CARF genes and CoCoNuTs typically coming last, although Druantia Type III sometimes follows the CoCoNuT.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8.

claim: Translation in bacteria is co-transcriptional, so products of genes transcribed first would accumulate before those of genes transcribed last.
source: As translation in bacteria is co-transcriptional, the products of genes transcribed first would accumulate before those of the genes transcribed last, so that the full, potentially suicidal impact of the CoCoNuT predicted RNA nucleolytic engine would only be felt after the associated DNA restriction systems had ample time to act – and possibly, fail (Irastortza-olaziregi and Amster-choder, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: BrnT-like RelE family RNase toxins are frequently encoded immediately upstream of RtcR-associated CoCoNuTs.
source: Another noteworthy observation consistent with PCD induction is the frequent presence of BrnT-like RelE family RNase toxins encoded in the same direction and immediately upstream of RtcR-associated CoCoNuTs (Figure 8, Figure 8—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8.

claim: In many species of Pseudomonas, Type I RM systems often contain an additional gene encoding ShdA, the core component of the Shield defense system.
source: In many species of Pseudomonas, where CoCoNuTs are almost always associated with RtcR and various ancillary factors, Type I RM systems often contain an additional gene that encodes a transmembrane helix and a long coiled-coil fused to an RmuC-like nuclease (Figure 8). These proteins were recently described as ShdA, the core component of the Pseudomonas-specific defense system Shield (Macdonald et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8, supported by a citation.

claim: Systematic searches for defense systems in prokaryotes revealed enormous, previously unsuspected diversity of such systems.
source: In recent years, systematic searches for defense systems in prokaryotes, primarily by analysis of defense islands, revealed enormous, previously unsuspected diversity of such systems that function through a remarkable variety of molecular mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusion section.

claim: This work uncovered the hidden diversity and striking hierarchical complexity of Type IV (McrBC) restriction systems.
source: In this work, we uncovered the hidden diversity and striking hierarchical complexity of a distinct class of defense mechanisms, the Type IV (McrBC) restriction systems.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusion section summarizing the findings.

claim: Astounding complexity was discovered at the CoCoNuT level, with three distinct types and multiple subtypes that differ by their domain compositions and genomic associations.
source: Astounding complexity was discovered at this level as well, with three distinct types and multiple subtypes of CoCoNuTs that differ by their domain compositions and genomic associations.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusion section summarizing the findings.
